name: Pansy
lede: Pansy is a deep violet-blue named for the flower; the older "pansy purple" was a naturalist's color in Patrick Syme's 1814 chart, and a different shade again.

sections.title: Which pansy
sections.body:
The swatch is a deep violet-blue, #3C2E73, the color Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* calls Pansy [1]. The NBS cited that book in 1955, and our library's note gives 1705 as its first recorded date, a date we could not check [1]. The nearest ISCC-NBS category is deep purplish blue, and the nearest learnable color is [[indigo]], 5.2 units away [1].

Paterson's dictionary defines pansy simply as a deep violet or purple, and also files it among the blues [2].

sections.title: Syme's pansy purple
sections.body:
The older use is Patrick Syme's [3]. In his 1814 *Werner's Nomenclature of Colours* he kept most of Abraham Werner's names but added two principal colors, purple and orange, and renamed Werner's violet blue and plum blue as violet purple and plum purple [3]. Syme was a flower painter, and his knowledge of flowers shows in pansy purple and auricula purple [3]. His book grew from 108 colors to 110 in the 1821 edition [3].

Baty's modern edition gives his recipe for pansy purple as a mix of indigo blue, carmine red and a faint touch of raven black [3]. It illustrates the color with the petals of a sweet violet, the back of a small bloody-nosed beetle and a fluorite crystal [3]. In Syme's order it sits between violet purple and campanula purple [3].

sections.title: Three pansies, three colors
sections.body:
The word does not fix one color. Our library carries Syme's swatch, as taken from Werner's tradition, as #39334A, a dark grey-violet [4]. Ridgway's Pansy Purple, from 1912, is #843751, a wine red-purple, and the library's own modern Pansy Purple is #78184A, close to [[byzantium]] [4]. The article's Pansy, from Maerz and Paul, is the bluest and most saturated of the three [1][4].

Paterson's two filings, among the purples and among the blues, fit this spread [2]. If a source says pansy, check which book it means before picturing the color. The color of that name has its own page: [[pansy-purple]].

sections.title: Pansy green
sections.body: The odd fact is that a pansy name once meant green. The Pigment Compendium cites Hilliard, who in 1624 described a pansy green, and a recipe in a British Library manuscript for making it from violet petals [5]. Thompson thinks the coloring matter in such plant greens is most likely chlorophyll [5]. Pansy green belongs with iris green and [[sap-green]] among the plant greens the Compendium lists [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of #3C2E73 covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 3 [6]. The largest share is Louis Welden Hawkins's *[[painting:commons-Q17492409|The Eiffel Tower]]* of 1900, at 22 per cent [6]. The others are Matisse's *Seville Still Life* of 1910, at 8 per cent, and an 1850 portrait of Berenguela of Leon by Francisco Prats y Velasco, at 6 per cent [6]. Two of the three are from the 1900s, a rate 9.5 times the archive's, though from so few paintings that it proves little [6]. In these paintings the color is a shadow tone about two times in three and a midtone the rest [6]. The caveat is the usual one: these are photographs of aged, varnished canvases, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [6].

openers: A pansy name once meant green: a 1600s recipe made pansy green from violet petals.
Syme, a flower painter, gave pansy purple a recipe: indigo, carmine and a touch of black.
